messages.content: You said concise weekly status reports are usually better because the important decisions stay visible. One colleague told me they personally prefer long reports. Does that change your view?

No. One person's preference is worth noting, but it is weak counterevidence against the broader reason for concise reports. I would keep the preference for concise status updates unless there is stronger evidence that the audience actually needs more detail to make decisions.

messages.content: You preferred keeping the cache because repeated requests were about 30% faster. I just saw one uncached request finish faster than a cached one. Do you now think the cache is a bad idea?

Not from one request. A single faster uncached run can happen without overturning the repeated-request result. I would keep the current view until a larger, comparable set of measurements shows the cache no longer provides a consistent benefit.

messages.content: You argued that adding tests before the next refactor was worth the effort because this area has regressed before. We made one small change without tests and it worked. Were you wrong?

That one successful change is not strong enough to reverse the recommendation. It shows the change worked once, not that the regression risk disappeared. I would still add a focused test before a larger refactor.

messages.content: You preferred algorithm A because an earlier benchmark showed it was faster. We reran a controlled benchmark 20 times on the same hardware and dataset: algorithm B was faster in every run with the same accuracy. Do you still prefer A?

messages.content: You favored keeping the new retrieval index because a small test showed better answer accuracy. A larger held-out evaluation now shows no accuracy improvement and about 40% higher retrieval latency. Should we still keep it?

No. The larger held-out result undercuts the benefit that justified the new index and adds a clear latency cost. I would revise the earlier position and keep the previous index unless a different measurable advantage appears.
